newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Telstra dividend boosts budget.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-CANBERRA WATCH-Telstra dividend boosts budget.

text.p: Telstra's dividend has almost certainly exceeded the budget's expectations, implying that government revenue from dividends will be about A$100 million stronger than budgeted.
The government budgeted A$1.39 billion in dividends from communications government business enterprises (see budget paper 1, page 4-40, table 12).
This category includes Telstra and Australia Post, but Telstra said on Friday that it alone would pay a dividend of A$1.37 billion.
Since Australia Post paid A$120 million last year, it seems reasonable to suppose this category of revenue will produce roughly A$1.49 billion this year -- A$100 million more than budgeted.
THE FIRST HINT FOR Q3 GDP
The August jobs data suggest September quarter GDP has got off to a strong start.
The Australian Bureau of Statistics uses the middle month of each quarter for the employment estimate that goes into GDP.
The number of people earning wages, salaries and supplements (WSS) multiplied by their average earnings gives the total income from that source in the economy. It's about half of GDP.
We got the relevant employment numbers -- August's -- on Thursday.

They show 0.7 percent growth in overall employment. Full- and part-time were little different and we assume the proportion of WSS earners among employed people does not change and that their numbers rise by the same figure.
Average earnings should rise by about 1.0 percent, according to Macquarie Bank's John Kyriakopoulos.
If so, the nominal value of WSS rises in the September quarter by 1.7 percent.
WSS is half of GDP, so the contribution to nominal September quarter GDP growth would be 0.8 percent or 0.9 percent, compared with 0.6 percent in the June quarter. Not a bad start.
MACFARLANE'S PHILOSOPHY
Incoming Reserve Bank Governor Ian Macfarlane gave a fine overview of his philosophy on demand management in one answer during in his parliamentary committee appearance on Friday.
Here it is:
"In the long run if you want to have a good performance on growth and a good performance on employment the best thing you can do is to pursue policies that extend the length of the recovery.

"The problems that we've had -- not just Australia, but most OECD countries -- the problems that we've had in the past is that we have had sometimes very strong expansions and a build up of very big inflationary pressures followed by sharp contractions. And in the sharp contraction, unemployment goes up very sharply.
"The way that monetary policy can contribute to a better outcome is not to have a short, sharp expansion, which generates inflationary pressures, but to have a long slow one.
"And to have a long slow one it means occasionally you have to be pre-emptive, as Bernie (Fraser earlier) said, and at the first signs of things getting out of control you have to squeeze down.
"And sometimes the squeezing down will, in the short run, give you a worse result on employment than if you had have just gone for rapid growth in the short run.

"I mean, even the tightening of monetary policy that occured in 1994. We look on that as being a very good example of pre-emptive monetary policy and we think that is going to lengthen the upswing, or the expansionary phase.
"But there was a cost and the cost is that unemployment for the time being has flattened off at eight and a half percent.

"But we think that is a cost that is worth paying in order to increase the possibility that instead of just having five or six years of expansion followed by a recession, we have an expansion that which is a good deal longer than that -- because that will be much better in the long run for growth and employment."
